verdicts.argument: Re-checked PFE:transcripts/2025Q3_transcript.md p.8-9 (Divan asked about 'pricing and market share dynamics'; Malik answered with share leadership 'on a TRx basis' and first-line share), PFE:companies/PFE/transcripts/2025Q2_transcript.md p.10 ('Attruby is taking some first-line share' and GTN pressure from contracting), and BBIO:earnings/2026-01-12_ef20062706_ex99-2.md p.29 (30-40%+ Attruby share forecast). All verified, all grade A where transcripts. So share loss itself is said. On the '51% revenue share vs TRx leadership' framing: the two are not in conflict. Revenue share mixes price and volume. Amvuttra is a higher-priced per-patient therapy, and its U.S. row includes hATTR-PN. Pfizer can hold TRx leadership and a ~51% revenue share at the same time, so the gap is not evidence that management misstated anything. What survives under my lens is the size of the stall, recomputed on H1 to avoid single-quarter noise. U.S. H1: Vyndaqel 1,975 vs 1,976 (PFE 10-Q p.38); Amvuttra U.S. 1,511.6 vs 559.3 (ALNY p.38); Attruby 403.0 vs 108.2 (BBIO p.56). Class revenue 3,889.6 vs 2,643.5 (+$1,246M, +47%). Vyndaqel took ~0% of that growth, and its revenue share went from 74.8% to 50.8%. Vyndaqel U.S. is ~$3.8B, about 10% of Pfizer U.S. revenue (37,078, 10-K file p.42), so a flat line in a +47% class is material. Pfizer has never put a number on it.
verdicts.correction: Narrowed finding: in H1 2026 the U.S. ATTR-CM class (Vyndaqel + Amvuttra U.S. + Attruby) grew ~$1.25B (+47%) while U.S. Vyndaqel revenue was flat. Vyndaqel's revenue share fell from ~75% to ~51%. This is revenue share, shaped by price and by Amvuttra's PN use, so it does not contradict Pfizer's TRx-share leadership claim. Pfizer has disclosed share pressure and contracting qualitatively but never sized either.

round2.conceded: Share loss and its causes (first-line share to Attruby, payer contracting) were said on the 2025Q2 and 2025Q3 calls, and rivals publish share forecasts. The existence of share loss is not new.
round2.held: The quantification is material and unsaid. Vyndaqel took ~0 of $1.25B of H1 U.S. class growth on a ~$3.8B U.S. product, and no Pfizer source sizes it.
round2.narrowed: Dropped the 'vs TRx leadership' contrast as a contradiction, because revenue share and TRx share can both be true. Moved the headline from a single quarter (Q2 69.6% to 50.8%) to H1 (74.8% to 50.8%) with class growth captured.

verdicts.argument: Settled whether any version is material. Verified PFE:companies/PFE/transcripts/2024Q4_transcript.md p.7 (grade A): the CFO guided 'a higher gross to net impact on our revenues for all drugs in the beginning of 2025' from the Part D redesign, sized as a net revenue headwind of about $1B. So the 2025 step (38.6% to 41.3%, ~$2.4B at the 2024 rate) is guided Part D plus Paxlovid/Comirnaty mix, and the two cannot be separated from the cited data. For 2026, I backed Q1 out of the H1 and Q2 columns on 10-Q 2026Q2 p.37 and p.5. Q1'26 deductions 8,258 on gross 19,973 = 41.3% vs Q1'25 8,133/19,427 = 41.9%, so Q1 narrowed 0.5 pt. Q2 widened (43.2% vs 41.4% headline; 40.4% vs 39.9% ex-returns). H1 ex-returns is flat (40.04% vs 40.01%). There is no 2026 trend: one quarter down, one up, and the H1 headline move is the returns line, which p.38 ties to Comirnaty's smaller returns-provision benefit and Nurtec. The chargeback rise (+$639M H1) is matched by falls in Medicare rebates (-$207M) and sales allowances (-$142M). That is a shift in composition across deduction lines (consistent with less Medicare rebate under the redesign and more contract and 340B pricing), with no net P&L effect so far. No version of c02 clears the materiality bar as an unsaid, ongoing revenue drag.
verdicts.correction: No material finding. At most a composition note: in H1 2026, chargebacks (+11.8% in Q2) replaced Medicare rebates and sales allowances inside a flat ex-returns deduction rate (~40.0%). The 2025 step-up was guided (~$1B Part D, 2024Q4 call p.7) and partly COVID mix.

round2.conceded: The 2025 38.6% to 41.3% step should be dropped, because it was guided on the 2024Q4 call (verified p.7). And c11's chargeback evidence belongs here, not as a separate finding.
round2.held: The other skeptic kept the 'H1 2026 chargeback-led widening' as non-obvious, but it fails on math: H1 ex-returns rate is flat, Q1 narrowed and Q2 widened, and chargeback growth is offset line for line. Being unasked does not make a non-move material.
round2.narrowed: From 'widening is a lumpy returns move' to 'no 2026 trend at all'. Q1'26 narrowed 0.5 pt, which round 1 did not show.

Re-checked 10-Q 2026Q2 p.27 and p.46. The Depo-Provera agreement-in-principle (June 2026) and the Chantix MDL agreement (March 2026) are both in the Q2 10-Q. The $867M figure on p.46 (non-GAAP adjustment for legal matters) vs $842M in Note 4 is a $25M difference, probably legal costs booked outside Other deductions; immaterial. Materiality of the remaining item: $842M is ~$0.15 pre-tax GAAP EPS but excluded from adjusted EPS, so it does not touch consensus. It is cash, though: product-liability settlements are paid, so it reduces free cash flow even though adjusted EPS ignores it. The filing does not tie the Q2 accrual to Depo-Provera, so the link stays an inference.

Material to GAAP EPS and cash, not to adjusted EPS. The Depo attribution is inferred.

overall: After round 2, two PFE items are both material and not said by management. First, U.S. Vyndaqel was flat in H1 2026 while the U.S. ATTR-CM class grew ~$1.25B (+47%), cutting its revenue share from ~75% to ~51% (narrowed c01, a revenue-share fact, not a contradiction of TRx leadership). Second, the unexplained doubling of legal charges to $842M in Q2 2026 next to an unsized Depo-Provera MDL settlement (c04), which matters for GAAP and cash but not adjusted EPS. No version of the gross-to-net story (c02/c11) survives: the 2025 step was guided and the 2026 ex-returns rate is flat.
